accounts.prose: This module is the shared call-classification adapter used by several resilience policies. It turns an invoked synchronous or promise-like operation into a tagged success/handled-failure result, emits timed success/failure observations, and provides a helper that converts the tag back into ordinary return/throw behavior.

referent.description: Executor module and its execution-result adapter functionality

qualifications: Implementation-based account from first-observed TypeScript source; it does not establish deployed runtime behavior.
The module has no associated earlier account in this session, and no nearby explanatory documentation was supplied.

accounts.prose: ExecuteWrapper.invoke awaits the supplied function. An unfiltered resolved value becomes {success}; a result matching resultFilter becomes handled failure {value}; a thrown value matching errorFilter becomes {error}; and an unhandled throw is rethrown immediately. Success and failure events carry elapsed duration, while failures additionally report handled status and the error/value reason.

referent.description: ExecuteWrapper invocation and classification behavior

qualifications: Both synchronous throws and asynchronous rejection enter the same catch because invocation is awaited inside try/catch.
Default filters reject every error/result, so ordinary results succeed and thrown errors propagate.

qualifications: Represents the three observable outcomes: success, filtered value, or filtered error.

qualifications: Defines FailureReason, ISuccessEvent, and IFailureEvent consumed here.

accounts.prose: Timing is conditional: no stopwatch is created unless at least one success or failure listener exists. It uses performance.now when available, otherwise process.hrtime.bigint converted to milliseconds. clone preserves the two filters but creates fresh emitters, isolating subscriptions between policy copies.

referent.description: Conditional timing, event emission, and cloning in ExecuteWrapper

qualifications: The environment-dependent clocks are implementation branches, not a precision guarantee.
Listener storage and dispatch are delegated to the Event module.

qualifications: Owns the EventEmitter implementation used by both channels.

accounts.prose: returnOrThrow reverses the tagged protocol: it throws an {error}, returns a {success}, and otherwise returns the filtered failure {value}. Thus callers decide whether a handled value remains a normal return, while handled errors regain exception semantics.

referent.description: returnOrThrow result-unwrapping helper

qualifications: The helper is intentionally mechanical; retry and other policies can inspect the union directly instead.

qualifications: NoopPolicy invokes through ExecuteWrapper and immediately delegates the tagged result to returnOrThrow.

accounts.prose: Policy factories supply configured wrappers to retry, circuit-breaker, and fallback policies. Retry repeatedly invokes through the wrapper, returns {success}, feeds handled failures into backoff/retry events, and on exhaustion throws {error} or returns {value}. NoopPolicy uses the wrapper only for classification/telemetry before unwrapping. BulkheadPolicy constructs a wrapper and exposes its listeners, but its shown execute path calls the function directly, so wrapper timing/classification is not applied there.

referent.description: Delegation from policy construction into consumers of ExecuteWrapper

qualifications: Retry, no-op, and bulkhead were inspected as representative consumers; fallback and circuit-breaker construction is established, but their full execution implementations were not read.
The bulkhead observation is limited to the supplied first-observed implementation source.

accounts.prose: `ExecuteWrapper.invoke` is a classifier around one function call, not the policy action itself. It starts optional timing, invokes and awaits `fn(...args)`, and then returns exactly one of three tagged shapes: `{ success: value }` for a resolved value rejected by `resultFilter`; `{ value }` for a resolved value accepted by `resultFilter`; or `{ error }` for a caught throw/rejection accepted by `errorFilter`. A caught item rejected by `errorFilter` is not converted into a result: a failure notification is attempted with `handled: false`, then the same thrown value is rethrown. Thus “handled” means selected by a configured filter for policy processing, not that the operation succeeded or that the reason was transformed.

`errorFilter` and the failure notification in the catch block are not protected by another local catch. If either throws, that new exception propagates and can supersede the originally caught reason.

accounts.prose: The resolved-value path first applies `resultFilter`. A false result emits success, when observable, and returns `{ success: value }`. A true result is deliberately represented as a handled failure: it emits `onFailure` with `handled: true` and `reason: { value }`, then returns `{ value }`. The thrown/rejected path applies `errorFilter`. A true result emits `handled: true` with `reason: { error }` and returns `{ error }`; a false result emits `handled: false` with the same reason and then rethrows. Synchronous throws and promise rejections converge because the call is awaited inside the `try`.

accounts.prose: Timing is demand-driven. At the start of `invoke`, a stopwatch is created only if either success or failure emitter currently has at least one listener. It uses `performance.now()` when available, otherwise `process.hrtime.bigint()`, and reports milliseconds. The measured interval includes the awaited call and the applicable filter evaluation, ending when the event object is prepared; listener execution itself occurs afterward. No event history is retained by these base emitters.

referent.description: ExecuteWrapper timing and event-observation mechanics

qualifications: If neither emitter has a listener when invocation begins, adding one while the operation is pending does not enable an event for that invocation because the stored stopwatch remains null.

If either emitter has a listener at invocation start, timing is enabled for the invocation even when the eventual outcome belongs to the other emitter; emitting to an emitter with no listeners is a no-op.
Listeners are called synchronously and listener exceptions are not isolated by EventEmitter.

@investigram-7a0a9dfa · interpretation
`ExecuteWrapper.invoke` is a classifier around one function call, not the policy action itself. It starts optional timing, invokes and awaits `fn(...args)`, and then returns exactly one of three tagged shapes: `{ success: value }` for a resolved value rejected by `resultFilter`; `{ value }` for a resolved value accepted by `resultFilter`; or `{ error }` for a caught throw/rejection accepted by `errorFilter`. A caught item rejected by `errorFilter` is not converted into a result: a failure notification is attempted with `handled: false`, then the same thrown value is rethrown. Thus “handled” means selected by a configured filter for policy processing, not that the operation succeeded or that the reason was transformed.
Referent: Clarified invocation, classification, timing, and notification behavior of ExecuteWrapper
  Qualification: This expands the earlier account rather than correcting it; its main outcome classification is consistent with the captured implementation.
  Qualification: The account is based on captured TypeScript source and compiler-derived symbol identity, not execution of the code.
  Qualification: The `try` block also contains result filtering and success/result-failure notification. Consequently, exceptions from `resultFilter` or from listeners invoked there enter the same catch path as an exception from `fn`; this is a sharp edge rather than the ordinary intended call outcome.
  Qualification: `errorFilter` and the failure notification in the catch block are not protected by another local catch. If either throws, that new exception propagates and can supersede the originally caught reason.

@investigram-a94d7314 · interpretation
The resolved-value path first applies `resultFilter`. A false result emits success, when observable, and returns `{ success: value }`. A true result is deliberately represented as a handled failure: it emits `onFailure` with `handled: true` and `reason: { value }`, then returns `{ value }`. The thrown/rejected path applies `errorFilter`. A true result emits `handled: true` with `reason: { error }` and returns `{ error }`; a false result emits `handled: false` with the same reason and then rethrows. Synchronous throws and promise rejections converge because the call is awaited inside the `try`.
Referent: Four classification branches within ExecuteWrapper.invoke
  Qualification: The filters are predicates only: they choose the branch but do not replace the resolved or thrown payload.
  Qualification: An unhandled exception can still produce an `onFailure` observation before propagation; “unhandled” means it is not returned as `{ error }`.
  Qualification: With constructor defaults, neither predicate selects anything, so resolved values become `{ success }` and ordinary caught exceptions are rethrown.

@investigram-e391831d · interpretation
Timing is demand-driven. At the start of `invoke`, a stopwatch is created only if either success or failure emitter currently has at least one listener. It uses `performance.now()` when available, otherwise `process.hrtime.bigint()`, and reports milliseconds. The measured interval includes the awaited call and the applicable filter evaluation, ending when the event object is prepared; listener execution itself occurs afterward. No event history is retained by these base emitters.
Referent: ExecuteWrapper timing and event-observation mechanics
  Qualification: If neither emitter has a listener when invocation begins, adding one while the operation is pending does not enable an event for that invocation because the stored stopwatch remains null.
  Qualification: If either emitter has a listener at invocation start, timing is enabled for the invocation even when the eventual outcome belongs to the other emitter; emitting to an emitter with no listeners is a no-op.
  Qualification: Listeners are called synchronously and listener exceptions are not isolated by EventEmitter.

@investigram-b1cc219c · interpretation
`clone()` creates a fresh wrapper that reuses the same two predicate function objects but has new success and failure emitters, so listeners are not copied. Separately, `returnOrThrow` converts a completed tagged outcome back to ordinary control flow: `{ error }` is thrown, while both `{ success }` and `{ value }` yield their payload. This separation lets policy implementations inspect handled failures before deciding whether and when to expose a value or throw.

accounts.prose: `ExecuteWrapper.invoke` is a classifier around one function call, not the policy action itself. It starts optional timing, invokes and awaits `fn(...args)`, and then returns exactly one of three tagged shapes: `{ success: value }` for a resolved value rejected by `resultFilter`; `{ value }` for a resolved value accepted by `resultFilter`; or `{ error }` for a caught throw/rejection accepted by `errorFilter`. A caught item rejected by `errorFilter` is not converted into a result: a failure notification is attempted with `handled: false`, then the same thrown value is rethrown. Thus “handled” means selected by a configured filter for policy processing, not that the operation succeeded or that the reason was transformed.

referent.description: Clarified invocation, classification, timing, and notification behavior of ExecuteWrapper

qualifications: This expands the earlier account rather than correcting it; its main outcome classification is consistent with the captured implementation.
The account is based on captured TypeScript source and compiler-derived symbol identity, not execution of the code.

The `try` block also contains result filtering and success/result-failure notification. Consequently, exceptions from `resultFilter` or from listeners invoked there enter the same catch path as an exception from `fn`; this is a sharp edge rather than the ordinary intended call outcome.
`errorFilter` and the failure notification in the catch block are not protected by another local catch. If either throws, that new exception propagates and can supersede the originally caught reason.

accounts.prose: The resolved-value path first applies `resultFilter`. A false result emits success, when observable, and returns `{ success: value }`. A true result is deliberately represented as a handled failure: it emits `onFailure` with `handled: true` and `reason: { value }`, then returns `{ value }`. The thrown/rejected path applies `errorFilter`. A true result emits `handled: true` with `reason: { error }` and returns `{ error }`; a false result emits `handled: false` with the same reason and then rethrows. Synchronous throws and promise rejections converge because the call is awaited inside the `try`.

accounts.prose: `clone()` creates a fresh wrapper that reuses the same two predicate function objects but has new success and failure emitters, so listeners are not copied. Separately, `returnOrThrow` converts a completed tagged outcome back to ordinary control flow: `{ error }` is thrown, while both `{ success }` and `{ value }` yield their payload. accounts.prose: `ExecuteWrapper.invoke` is a classifier around one function call, not the policy action itself. It starts optional timing, invokes and awaits `fn(...args)`, and then returns exactly one of three tagged shapes: `{ success: value }` for a resolved value rejected by `resultFilter`; `{ value }` for a resolved value accepted by `resultFilter`; or `{ error }` for a caught throw/rejection accepted by `errorFilter`. A caught item rejected by `errorFilter` is not converted into a result: a failure notification is attempted with `handled: false`, then the same thrown value is rethrown. Thus “handled” means selected by a configured filter for policy processing, not that the operation succeeded or that the reason was transformed.

referent.description: Clarified invocation, classification, timing, and notification behavior of ExecuteWrapper

qualifications: This expands the earlier account rather than correcting it; its main outcome classification is consistent with the captured implementation.
The account is based on captured TypeScript source and compiler-derived symbol identity, not execution of the code.

The `try` block also contains result filtering and success/result-failure notification. Consequently, exceptions from `resultFilter` or from listeners invoked there enter the same catch path as an exception from `fn`; this is a sharp edge rather than the ordinary intended call outcome.
`errorFilter` and the failure notification in the catch block are not protected by another local catch. If either throws, that new exception propagates and can supersede the originally caught reason.

accounts.prose: The resolved-value path first applies `resultFilter`. A false result emits success, when observable, and returns `{ success: value }`. A true result is deliberately represented as a handled failure: it emits `onFailure` with `handled: true` and `reason: { value }`, then returns `{ value }`. The thrown/rejected path applies `errorFilter`. A true result emits `handled: true` with `reason: { error }` and returns `{ error }`; a false result emits `handled: false` with the same reason and then rethrows. Synchronous throws and promise rejections converge because the call is awaited inside the `try`.

qualifications: The filters are predicates only: they choose the branch but do not replace the resolved or thrown payload.
An unhandled exception can still produce an `onFailure` observation before propagation; “unhandled” means it is not returned as `{ error }`.

accounts.prose: `ExecuteWrapper.invoke` is a classifier around one function call, not the policy action itself. It starts optional timing, invokes and awaits `fn(...args)`, and then returns exactly one of three tagged shapes: `{ success: value }` for a resolved value rejected by `resultFilter`; `{ value }` for a resolved value accepted by `resultFilter`; or `{ error }` for a caught throw/rejection accepted by `errorFilter`. A caught item rejected by `errorFilter` is not converted into a result: a failure notification is attempted with `handled: false`, then the same thrown value is rethrown. Thus “handled” means selected by a configured filter for policy processing, not that the operation succeeded or that the reason was transformed.

referent.description: Clarified invocation, classification, timing, and notification behavior of ExecuteWrapper

qualifications: This expands the earlier account rather than correcting it; its main outcome classification is consistent with the captured implementation.
The account is based on captured TypeScript source and compiler-derived symbol identity, not execution of the code.

The `try` block also contains result filtering and success/result-failure notification. Consequently, exceptions from `resultFilter` or from listeners invoked there enter the same catch path as an exception from `fn`; this is a sharp edge rather than the ordinary intended call outcome.
`errorFilter` and the failure notification in the catch block are not protected by another local catch. If either throws, that new exception propagates and can supersede the originally caught reason.

accounts.prose: The resolved-value path first applies `resultFilter`. A false result emits success, when observable, and returns `{ success: value }`. A true result is deliberately represented as a handled failure: it emits `onFailure` with `handled: true` and `reason: { value }`, then returns `{ value }`. The thrown/rejected path applies `errorFilter`. A true result emits `handled: true` with `reason: { error }` and returns `{ error }`; a false result emits `handled: false` with the same reason and then rethrows. Synchronous throws and promise rejections converge because the call is awaited inside the `try`.

qualifications: The filters are predicates only: they choose the branch but do not replace the resolved or thrown payload.
An unhandled exception can still produce an `onFailure` observation before propagation; “unhandled” means it is not returned as `{ error }`.
With constructor defaults, neither predicate selects anything, so resolved values become `{ success }` and ordinary caught exceptions are rethrown.

accounts.prose: Timing is demand-driven. At the start of `invoke`, a stopwatch is created only if either success or failure emitter currently has at least one listener. It uses `performance.now()` when available, otherwise `process.hrtime.bigint()`, and reports milliseconds. The measured interval includes the awaited call and the applicable filter evaluation, ending when the event object is prepared; listener execution itself occurs afterward. No event history is retained by these base emitters.

referent.description: ExecuteWrapper timing and event-observation mechanics

qualifications: If neither emitter has a listener when invocation begins, adding one while the operation is pending does not enable an event for that invocation because the stored stopwatch remains null.

If either emitter has a listener at invocation start, timing is enabled for the invocation even when the eventual outcome belongs to the other emitter; emitting to an emitter with no listeners is a no-op.
Listeners are called synchronously and listener exceptions are not isolated by EventEmitter.

accounts.prose: `ExecuteWrapper.invoke` has a broader error boundary than “errors from the invoked operation”: its `try` also encloses resolved-value filtering and success notification. Any synchronous throw or awaited rejection from those steps is passed to `errorFilter`. The resulting boolean is recorded in a failure event before the method either returns `{ error }` when handled or rethrows the original caught value when unhandled. This classification is not recursively protected: exceptions from `errorFilter`, elapsed-time calculation, or synchronous failure listeners escape directly and can prevent or replace the intended `{ error }`/rethrow outcome.

referent.description: Detailed control-flow, observability, and secondary-failure behavior of caught-value classification in ExecuteWrapper.invoke

qualifications: This is a static interpretation of first-observed TypeScript source, not executed or deployed-runtime evidence.
The caught value is typed `unknown`; neither classification nor propagation requires an `Error` instance.
The constructor's default `errorFilter` returns false, but policy factories shown in the supplied Policy source normally construct wrappers with explicit policy filters.
Failure notification is synchronous and occurs before the final return or rethrow; a throwing listener therefore changes the externally observed outcome.

The supplied focused tests cover ordinary handled and unhandled `Error` instances, but not non-Error throws, filter exceptions, listener exceptions, or errors originating in resolved-value filtering or success listeners.

accounts.prose: `ExecuteWrapper.invoke` is a classifier around one function call, not the policy action itself. It starts optional timing, invokes and awaits `fn(...args)`, and then returns exactly one of three tagged shapes: `{ success: value }` for a resolved value rejected by `resultFilter`; `{ value }` for a resolved value accepted by `resultFilter`; or `{ error }` for a caught throw/rejection accepted by `errorFilter`. A caught item rejected by `errorFilter` is not converted into a result: a failure notification is attempted with `handled: false`, then the same thrown value is rethrown. Thus “handled” means selected by a configured filter for policy processing, not that the operation succeeded or that the reason was transformed.

referent.description: Clarified invocation, classification, timing, and notification behavior of ExecuteWrapper

qualifications: This expands the earlier account rather than correcting it; its main outcome classification is consistent with the captured implementation.

The `try` block also contains result filtering and success/result-failure notification. Consequently, exceptions from `resultFilter` or from listeners invoked there enter the same catch path as an exception from `fn`; this is a sharp edge rather than the ordinary intended call outcome.
`errorFilter` and the failure notification in the catch block are not protected by another local catch. If either throws, that new exception propagates and can supersede the originally caught reason.

accounts.prose: The resolved-value path first applies `resultFilter`. A false result emits success, when observable, and returns `{ success: value }`. A true result is deliberately represented as a handled failure: it emits `onFailure` with `handled: true` and `reason: { value }`, then returns `{ value }`. The thrown/rejected path applies `errorFilter`. A true result emits `handled: true` with `reason: { error }` and returns `{ error }`; a false result emits `handled: false` with the same reason and then rethrows. Synchronous throws and promise rejections converge because the call is awaited inside the `try`.

referent.description: Four classification branches within ExecuteWrapper.invoke

qualifications: The filters are predicates only: they choose the branch but do not replace the resolved or thrown payload.
An unhandled exception can still produce an `onFailure` observation before propagation; “unhandled” means it is not returned as `{ error }`.
With constructor defaults, neither predicate selects anything, so resolved values become `{ success }` and ordinary caught exceptions are rethrown.

accounts.prose: Timing is demand-driven. At the start of `invoke`, a stopwatch is created only if either success or failure emitter currently has at least one listener. It uses `performance.now()` when available, otherwise `process.hrtime.bigint()`, and reports milliseconds. The measured interval includes the awaited call and the applicable filter evaluation, ending when the event object is prepared; listener execution itself occurs afterward. No event history is retained by these base emitters.

referent.description: ExecuteWrapper timing and event-observation mechanics

qualifications: If neither emitter has a listener when invocation begins, adding one while the operation is pending does not enable an event for that invocation because the stored stopwatch remains null.

If either emitter has a listener at invocation start, timing is enabled for the invocation even when the eventual outcome belongs to the other emitter; emitting to an emitter with no listeners is a no-op.
Listeners are called synchronously and listener exceptions are not isolated by EventEmitter.

accounts.prose: `clone()` creates a fresh wrapper that reuses the same two predicate function objects but has new success and failure emitters, so listeners are not copied. Separately, `returnOrThrow` converts a completed tagged outcome back to ordinary control flow: `{ error }` is thrown, while both `{ success }` and `{ value }` yield their payload. This separation lets policy implementations inspect handled failures before deciding whether and when to expose a value or throw.

accounts.prose: ExecuteWrapper.invoke awaits the supplied function. An unfiltered resolved value becomes {success}; a result matching resultFilter becomes handled failure {value}; a thrown value matching errorFilter becomes {error}; and an unhandled throw is rethrown immediately. Success and failure events carry elapsed duration, while failures additionally report handled status and the error/value reason.

@investigram-a3ed2fe4 · interpretation
`ExecuteWrapper.invoke` has a broader error boundary than “errors from the invoked operation”: its `try` also encloses resolved-value filtering and success notification. Any synchronous throw or awaited rejection from those steps is passed to `errorFilter`. The resulting boolean is recorded in a failure event before the method either returns `{ error }` when handled or rethrows the original caught value when unhandled. This classification is not recursively protected: exceptions from `errorFilter`, elapsed-time calculation, or synchronous failure listeners escape directly and can prevent or replace the intended `{ error }`/rethrow outcome.
Referent: Detailed control-flow, observability, and secondary-failure behavior of caught-value classification in ExecuteWrapper.invoke
  Qualification: This is a static interpretation of first-observed TypeScript source, not executed or deployed-runtime evidence.
  Qualification: The caught value is typed `unknown`; neither classification nor propagation requires an `Error` instance.
  Qualification: The constructor's default `errorFilter` returns false, but policy factories shown in the supplied Policy source normally construct wrappers with explicit policy filters.
  Qualification: Failure notification is synchronous and occurs before the final return or rethrow; a throwing listener therefore changes the externally observed outcome.
  Qualification: The supplied focused tests cover ordinary handled and unhandled `Error` instances, but not non-Error throws, filter exceptions, listener exceptions, or errors originating in resolved-value filtering or success listeners.

@investigram-860ecfdf · interpretation
The catch boundary includes `await fn(...args)`, `resultFilter(value)`, elapsed-time measurement on the success path, and synchronous success-event emission. Consequently, an error caused by classification or observation infrastructure is indistinguishable at this boundary from an operation rejection and may itself be selected as a handled policy failure.
Referent: Operations whose exceptions enter caught-value classification
  Qualification: Only statements lexically inside the implementation's `try` enter this catch; setup before the `try`, including conditional stopwatch creation, does not.
  Qualification: A listener exception can be classified only for success-event emission inside the try; failure-event emission occurs inside the catch and is not caught again.

@investigram-802c57e4 · interpretation
Within the catch, `errorFilter` runs first. If it returns normally, `invoke` emits one failure event when timing was enabled, with the same caught value in `reason.error` and the computed `handled` flag. It then rethrows that exact value when false or returns `{ error }` when true.
Referent: Ordering and data flow inside ExecuteWrapper.invoke's catch block
  Qualification: Timing is enabled only if at least one success or failure listener existed when invocation began; later listener changes do not alter whether this invocation has a stopwatch.
  Qualification: The event is attempted for both handled and unhandled values when timing is enabled.
  Qualification: “One failure event” describes one `emit` call; multiple registered listeners may each receive it.

@investigram-c4293f15 · interpretation
The catch body has no nested protection. If `errorFilter` throws, no failure event is emitted and its exception escapes. If duration calculation or a failure listener throws, that secondary exception escapes before the intended handled return or original-value rethrow; with multiple listeners, synchronous iteration also stops at the throwing listener.

  Qualification: The claim concerns direct control flow in the supplied implementations; no runtime experiment was performed.
  Qualification: A secondary failure can mask the originally caught value from the caller, although earlier listeners may already have observed the failure event.
  Qualification: The focused Executor tests do not exercise these secondary-failure cases.

accounts.prose: `ExecuteWrapper.invoke` is a classifier around one function call, not the policy action itself. It starts optional timing, invokes and awaits `fn(...args)`, and then returns exactly one of three tagged shapes: `{ success: value }` for a resolved value rejected by `resultFilter`; `{ value }` for a resolved value accepted by `resultFilter`; or `{ error }` for a caught throw/rejection accepted by `errorFilter`. A caught item rejected by `errorFilter` is not converted into a result: a failure notification is attempted with `handled: false`, then the same thrown value is rethrown. Thus “handled” means selected by a configured filter for policy processing, not that the operation succeeded or that the reason was transformed.

referent.description: Clarified invocation, classification, timing, and notification behavior of ExecuteWrapper

qualifications: This expands the earlier account rather than correcting it; its main outcome classification is consistent with the captured implementation.
The account is based on captured TypeScript source and compiler-derived symbol identity, not execution of the code.

The `try` block also contains result filtering and success/result-failure notification. Consequently, exceptions from `resultFilter` or from listeners invoked there enter the same catch path as an exception from `fn`; this is a sharp edge rather than the ordinary intended call outcome.
`errorFilter` and the failure notification in the catch block are not protected by another local catch. If either throws, that new exception propagates and can supersede the originally caught reason.

accounts.prose: The resolved-value path first applies `resultFilter`. A false result emits success, when observable, and returns `{ success: value }`. A true result is deliberately represented as a handled failure: it emits `onFailure` with `handled: true` and `reason: { value }`, then returns `{ value }`. The thrown/rejected path applies `errorFilter`. A true result emits `handled: true` with `reason: { error }` and returns `{ error }`; a false result emits `handled: false` with the same reason and then rethrows. Synchronous throws and promise rejections converge because the call is awaited inside the `try`.

referent.description: Four classification branches within ExecuteWrapper.invoke

qualifications: The filters are predicates only: they choose the branch but do not replace the resolved or thrown payload.
An unhandled exception can still produce an `onFailure` observation before propagation; “unhandled” means it is not returned as `{ error }`.
With constructor defaults, neither predicate selects anything, so resolved values become `{ success }` and ordinary caught exceptions are rethrown.

accounts.prose: Timing is demand-driven. At the start of `invoke`, a stopwatch is created only if either success or failure emitter currently has at least one listener. It uses `performance.now()` when available, otherwise `process.hrtime.bigint()`, and reports milliseconds. The measured interval includes the awaited call and the applicable filter evaluation, ending when the event object is prepared; listener execution itself occurs afterward. No event history is retained by these base emitters.

referent.description: ExecuteWrapper timing and event-observation mechanics

qualifications: If neither emitter has a listener when invocation begins, adding one while the operation is pending does not enable an event for that invocation because the stored stopwatch remains null.

If either emitter has a listener at invocation start, timing is enabled for the invocation even when the eventual outcome belongs to the other emitter; emitting to an emitter with no listeners is a no-op.
Listeners are called synchronously and listener exceptions are not isolated by EventEmitter.

accounts.prose: `clone()` creates a fresh wrapper that reuses the same two predicate function objects but has new success and failure emitters, so listeners are not copied. Separately, `returnOrThrow` converts a completed tagged outcome back to ordinary control flow: `{ error }` is thrown, while both `{ success }` and `{ value }` yield their payload. This separation lets policy implementations inspect handled failures before deciding whether and when to expose a value or throw.

referent.description: ExecuteWrapper cloning and conversion of classified outcomes

qualifications: Sharing predicate functions does not imply copying any external mutable state those functions may close over.
The final sentence describes the mechanism enabled by the separation; individual policy decisions were not exhaustively inspected here.

An unfiltered resolved value becomes {success}; a result matching resultFilter becomes handled failure {value}; a thrown value matching errorFilter becomes {error}; and an unhandled throw is rethrown immediately. Success and failure events carry elapsed duration, while failures additionally report handled status and the error/value reason.

referent.description: ExecuteWrapper invocation and classification behavior

qualifications: Both synchronous throws and asynchronous rejection enter the same catch because invocation is awaited inside try/catch.
Default filters reject every error/result, so ordinary results succeed and thrown errors propagate.

accounts.prose: `ExecuteWrapper.invoke` is a classifier around one function call, not the policy action itself. It starts optional timing, invokes and awaits `fn(...args)`, and then returns exactly one of three tagged shapes: `{ success: value }` for a resolved value rejected by `resultFilter`; `{ value }` for a resolved value accepted by `resultFilter`; or `{ error }` for a caught throw/rejection accepted by `errorFilter`. A caught item rejected by `errorFilter` is not converted into a result: a failure notification is attempted with `handled: false`, then the same thrown value is rethrown. Thus “handled” means selected by a configured filter for policy processing, not that the operation succeeded or that the reason was transformed.

referent.description: Clarified invocation, classification, timing, and notification behavior of ExecuteWrapper

qualifications: This expands the earlier account rather than correcting it; its main outcome classification is consistent with the captured implementation.
The account is based on captured TypeScript source and compiler-derived symbol identity, not execution of the code.

The `try` block also contains result filtering and success/result-failure notification. Consequently, exceptions from `resultFilter` or from listeners invoked there enter the same catch path as an exception from `fn`; this is a sharp edge rather than the ordinary intended call outcome.
`errorFilter` and the failure notification in the catch block are not protected by another local catch. If either throws, that new exception propagates and can supersede the originally caught reason.

accounts.prose: The resolved-value path first applies `resultFilter`. A false result emits success, when observable, and returns `{ success: value }`. A true result is deliberately represented as a handled failure: it emits `onFailure` with `handled: true` and `reason: { value }`, then returns `{ value }`. The thrown/rejected path applies `errorFilter`. A true result emits `handled: true` with `reason: { error }` and returns `{ error }`; a false result emits `handled: false` with the same reason and then rethrows. Synchronous throws and promise rejections converge because the call is awaited inside the `try`.

referent.description: Four classification branches within ExecuteWrapper.invoke

qualifications: The filters are predicates only: they choose the branch but do not replace the resolved or thrown payload.
An unhandled exception can still produce an `onFailure` observation before propagation; “unhandled” means it is not returned as `{ error }`.
With constructor defaults, neither predicate selects anything, so resolved values become `{ success }` and ordinary caught exceptions are rethrown.

accounts.prose: Timing is demand-driven. At the start of `invoke`, a stopwatch is created only if either success or failure emitter currently has at least one listener. It uses `performance.now()` when available, otherwise `process.hrtime.bigint()`, and reports milliseconds. The measured interval includes the awaited call and the applicable filter evaluation, ending when the event object is prepared; listener execution itself occurs afterward. No event history is retained by these base emitters.

referent.description: ExecuteWrapper timing and event-observation mechanics

qualifications: If neither emitter has a listener when invocation begins, adding one while the operation is pending does not enable an event for that invocation because the stored stopwatch remains null.

If either emitter has a listener at invocation start, timing is enabled for the invocation even when the eventual outcome belongs to the other emitter; emitting to an emitter with no listeners is a no-op.
Listeners are called synchronously and listener exceptions are not isolated by EventEmitter.

accounts.prose: `clone()` creates a fresh wrapper that reuses the same two predicate function objects but has new success and failure emitters, so listeners are not copied. Separately, `returnOrThrow` converts a completed tagged outcome back to ordinary control flow: `{ error }` is thrown, while both `{ success }` and `{ value }` yield their payload. This separation lets policy implementations inspect handled failures before deciding whether and when to expose a value or throw.

referent.description: ExecuteWrapper cloning and conversion of classified outcomes

qualifications: Sharing predicate functions does not imply copying any external mutable state those functions may close over.
The final sentence describes the mechanism enabled by the separation; individual policy decisions were not exhaustively inspected here.

It turns an invoked synchronous or promise-like operation into a tagged success/handled-failure result, emits timed success/failure observations, and provides a helper that converts the tag back into ordinary return/throw behavior.

@investigram-f0c3a29d · interpretation
ExecuteWrapper.invoke awaits the supplied function. An unfiltered resolved value becomes {success}; a result matching resultFilter becomes handled failure {value}; a thrown value matching errorFilter becomes {error}; and an unhandled throw is rethrown immediately. Success and failure events carry elapsed duration, while failures additionally report handled status and the error/value reason.
Referent: ExecuteWrapper invocation and classification behavior
  Qualification: Both synchronous throws and asynchronous rejection enter the same catch because invocation is awaited inside try/catch.
  Qualification: Default filters reject every error/result, so ordinary results succeed and thrown errors propagate.

It uses performance.now when available, otherwise process.hrtime.bigint converted to milliseconds. clone preserves the two filters but creates fresh emitters, isolating subscriptions between policy copies.

@investigram-cbe246c3 · interpretation
returnOrThrow reverses the tagged protocol: it throws an {error}, returns a {success}, and otherwise returns the filtered failure {value}. Thus callers decide whether a handled value remains a normal return, while handled errors regain exception semantics.
Referent: returnOrThrow result-unwrapping helper
  Qualification: The helper is intentionally mechanical; retry and other policies can inspect the union directly instead.

@investigram-e946c605 · interpretation
Policy factories supply configured wrappers to retry, circuit-breaker, and fallback policies. Retry repeatedly invokes through the wrapper, returns {success}, feeds handled failures into backoff/retry events, and on exhaustion throws {error} or returns {value}. NoopPolicy uses the wrapper only for classification/telemetry before unwrapping. BulkheadPolicy constructs a wrapper and exposes its listeners, but its shown execute path calls the function directly, so wrapper timing/classification is not applied there.
Referent: Delegation from policy construction into consumers of ExecuteWrapper

accounts.prose: `ExecuteWrapper.invoke` is a classifier around one function call, not the policy action itself. It starts optional timing, invokes and awaits `fn(...args)`, and then returns exactly one of three tagged shapes: `{ success: value }` for a resolved value rejected by `resultFilter`; `{ value }` for a resolved value accepted by `resultFilter`; or `{ error }` for a caught throw/rejection accepted by `errorFilter`. A caught item rejected by `errorFilter` is not converted into a result: a failure notification is attempted with `handled: false`, then the same thrown value is rethrown. Thus “handled” means selected by a configured filter for policy processing, not that the operation succeeded or that the reason was transformed.

referent.description: Clarified invocation, classification, timing, and notification behavior of ExecuteWrapper

accounts.prose: The resolved-value path first applies `resultFilter`. A false result emits success, when observable, and returns `{ success: value }`. A true result is deliberately represented as a handled failure: it emits `onFailure` with `handled: true` and `reason: { value }`, then returns `{ value }`. The thrown/rejected path applies `errorFilter`. A true result emits `handled: true` with `reason: { error }` and returns `{ error }`; a false result emits `handled: false` with the same reason and then rethrows. Synchronous throws and promise rejections converge because the call is awaited inside the `try`.

referent.description: Four classification branches within ExecuteWrapper.invoke

qualifications: The filters are predicates only: they choose the branch but do not replace the resolved or thrown payload.
An unhandled exception can still produce an `onFailure` observation before propagation; “unhandled” means it is not returned as `{ error }`.
With constructor defaults, neither predicate selects anything, so resolved values become `{ success }` and ordinary caught exceptions are rethrown.

accounts.prose: Timing is demand-driven. At the start of `invoke`, a stopwatch is created only if either success or failure emitter currently has at least one listener. It uses `performance.now()` when available, otherwise `process.hrtime.bigint()`, and reports milliseconds. The measured interval includes the awaited call and the applicable filter evaluation, ending when the event object is prepared; listener execution itself occurs afterward. No event history is retained by these base emitters.

referent.description: ExecuteWrapper timing and event-observation mechanics

qualifications: If neither emitter has a listener when invocation begins, adding one while the operation is pending does not enable an event for that invocation because the stored stopwatch remains null.

If either emitter has a listener at invocation start, timing is enabled for the invocation even when the eventual outcome belongs to the other emitter; emitting to an emitter with no listeners is a no-op.
Listeners are called synchronously and listener exceptions are not isolated by EventEmitter.

accounts.prose: `clone()` creates a fresh wrapper that reuses the same two predicate function objects but has new success and failure emitters, so listeners are not copied. Separately, `returnOrThrow` converts a completed tagged outcome back to ordinary control flow: `{ error }` is thrown, while both `{ success }` and `{ value }` yield their payload. This separation lets policy implementations inspect handled failures before deciding whether and when to expose a value or throw.

qualifications: Sharing predicate functions does not imply copying any external mutable state those functions may close over.

accounts.prose: `ExecuteWrapper.invoke` is a classifier around one function call, not the policy action itself. It starts optional timing, invokes and awaits `fn(...args)`, and then returns exactly one of three tagged shapes: `{ success: value }` for a resolved value rejected by `resultFilter`; `{ value }` for a resolved value accepted by `resultFilter`; or `{ error }` for a caught throw/rejection accepted by `errorFilter`. A caught item rejected by `errorFilter` is not converted into a result: a failure notification is attempted with `handled: false`, then the same thrown value is rethrown. Thus “handled” means selected by a configured filter for policy processing, not that the operation succeeded or that the reason was transformed.

referent.description: Clarified invocation, classification, timing, and notification behavior of ExecuteWrapper

qualifications: This expands the earlier account rather than correcting it; its main outcome classification is consistent with the captured implementation.
The account is based on captured TypeScript source and compiler-derived symbol identity, not execution of the code.

The `try` block also contains result filtering and success/result-failure notification. Consequently, exceptions from `resultFilter` or from listeners invoked there enter the same catch path as an exception from `fn`; this is a sharp edge rather than the ordinary intended call outcome.
`errorFilter` and the failure notification in the catch block are not protected by another local catch. If either throws, that new exception propagates and can supersede the originally caught reason.

accounts.prose: The resolved-value path first applies `resultFilter`. A false result emits success, when observable, and returns `{ success: value }`. A true result is deliberately represented as a handled failure: it emits `onFailure` with `handled: true` and `reason: { value }`, then returns `{ value }`. The thrown/rejected path applies `errorFilter`. A true result emits `handled: true` with `reason: { error }` and returns `{ error }`; a false result emits `handled: false` with the same reason and then rethrows. Synchronous throws and promise rejections converge because the call is awaited inside the `try`.

referent.description: Four classification branches within ExecuteWrapper.invoke

qualifications: The filters are predicates only: they choose the branch but do not replace the resolved or thrown payload.
An unhandled exception can still produce an `onFailure` observation before propagation; “unhandled” means it is not returned as `{ error }`.
With constructor defaults, neither predicate selects anything, so resolved values become `{ success }` and ordinary caught exceptions are rethrown.

accounts.prose: Timing is demand-driven. At the start of `invoke`, a stopwatch is created only if either success or failure emitter currently has at least one listener. It uses `performance.now()` when available, otherwise `process.hrtime.bigint()`, and reports milliseconds. The measured interval includes the awaited call and the applicable filter evaluation, ending when the event object is prepared; listener execution itself occurs afterward. No event history is retained by these base emitters.

referent.description: ExecuteWrapper timing and event-observation mechanics

qualifications: If neither emitter has a listener when invocation begins, adding one while the operation is pending does not enable an event for that invocation because the stored stopwatch remains null.

If either emitter has a listener at invocation start, timing is enabled for the invocation even when the eventual outcome belongs to the other emitter; emitting to an emitter with no listeners is a no-op.
Listeners are called synchronously and listener exceptions are not isolated by EventEmitter.

accounts.prose: `clone()` creates a fresh wrapper that reuses the same two predicate function objects but has new success and failure emitters, so listeners are not copied. Separately, `returnOrThrow` converts a completed tagged outcome back to ordinary control flow: `{ error }` is thrown, while both `{ success }` and `{ value }` yield their payload. This separation lets policy implementations inspect handled failures before deciding whether and when to expose a value or throw.

referent.description: ExecuteWrapper cloning and conversion of classified outcomes

qualifications: Sharing predicate functions does not imply copying any external mutable state those functions may close over.
The final sentence describes the mechanism enabled by the separation; individual policy decisions were not exhaustively inspected here.

accounts.prose: `ExecuteWrapper.invoke` is a classifier around one function call, not the policy action itself. It starts optional timing, invokes and awaits `fn(...args)`, and then returns exactly one of three tagged shapes: `{ success: value }` for a resolved value rejected by `resultFilter`; `{ value }` for a resolved value accepted by `resultFilter`; or `{ error }` for a caught throw/rejection accepted by `errorFilter`. A caught item rejected by `errorFilter` is not converted into a result: a failure notification is attempted with `handled: false`, then the same thrown value is rethrown. Thus “handled” means selected by a configured filter for policy processing, not that the operation succeeded or that the reason was transformed.

referent.description: Clarified invocation, classification, timing, and notification behavior of ExecuteWrapper

qualifications: This expands the earlier account rather than correcting it; its main outcome classification is consistent with the captured implementation.
The account is based on captured TypeScript source and compiler-derived symbol identity, not execution of the code.

The `try` block also contains result filtering and success/result-failure notification. Consequently, exceptions from `resultFilter` or from listeners invoked there enter the same catch path as an exception from `fn`; this is a sharp edge rather than the ordinary intended call outcome.
`errorFilter` and the failure notification in the catch block are not protected by another local catch. If either throws, that new exception propagates and can supersede the originally caught reason.

accounts.prose: The resolved-value path first applies `resultFilter`. A false result emits success, when observable, and returns `{ success: value }`. A true result is deliberately represented as a handled failure: it emits `onFailure` with `handled: true` and `reason: { value }`, then returns `{ value }`. The thrown/rejected path applies `errorFilter`. A true result emits `handled: true` with `reason: { error }` and returns `{ error }`; a false result emits `handled: false` with the same reason and then rethrows. Synchronous throws and promise rejections converge because the call is awaited inside the `try`.

referent.description: Four classification branches within ExecuteWrapper.invoke

qualifications: The filters are predicates only: they choose the branch but do not replace the resolved or thrown payload.
An unhandled exception can still produce an `onFailure` observation before propagation; “unhandled” means it is not returned as `{ error }`.
With constructor defaults, neither predicate selects anything, so resolved values become `{ success }` and ordinary caught exceptions are rethrown.

accounts.prose: Timing is demand-driven. At the start of `invoke`, a stopwatch is created only if either success or failure emitter currently has at least one listener. It uses `performance.now()` when available, otherwise `process.hrtime.bigint()`, and reports milliseconds. The measured interval includes the awaited call and the applicable filter evaluation, ending when the event object is prepared; listener execution itself occurs afterward. No event history is retained by these base emitters.

referent.description: ExecuteWrapper timing and event-observation mechanics

qualifications: If neither emitter has a listener when invocation begins, adding one while the operation is pending does not enable an event for that invocation because the stored stopwatch remains null.

If either emitter has a listener at invocation start, timing is enabled for the invocation even when the eventual outcome belongs to the other emitter; emitting to an emitter with no listeners is a no-op.
Listeners are called synchronously and listener exceptions are not isolated by EventEmitter.

accounts.prose: `clone()` creates a fresh wrapper that reuses the same two predicate function objects but has new success and failure emitters, so listeners are not copied. Separately, `returnOrThrow` converts a completed tagged outcome back to ordinary control flow: `{ error }` is thrown, while both `{ success }` and `{ value }` yield their payload. This separation lets policy implementations inspect handled failures before deciding whether and when to expose a value or throw.

referent.description: ExecuteWrapper cloning and conversion of classified outcomes

qualifications: Sharing predicate functions does not imply copying any external mutable state those functions may close over.
The final sentence describes the mechanism enabled by the separation; individual policy decisions were not exhaustively inspected here.

accounts.prose: `ExecuteWrapper.invoke` is a classifier around one function call, not the policy action itself. It starts optional timing, invokes and awaits `fn(...args)`, and then returns exactly one of three tagged shapes: `{ success: value }` for a resolved value rejected by `resultFilter`; `{ value }` for a resolved value accepted by `resultFilter`; or `{ error }` for a caught throw/rejection accepted by `errorFilter`. A caught item rejected by `errorFilter` is not converted into a result: a failure notification is attempted with `handled: false`, then the same thrown value is rethrown. Thus “handled” means selected by a configured filter for policy processing, not that the operation succeeded or that the reason was transformed.

referent.description: Clarified invocation, classification, timing, and notification behavior of ExecuteWrapper

qualifications: This expands the earlier account rather than correcting it; its main outcome classification is consistent with the captured implementation.
The account is based on captured TypeScript source and compiler-derived symbol identity, not execution of the code.

The `try` block also contains result filtering and success/result-failure notification. Consequently, exceptions from `resultFilter` or from listeners invoked there enter the same catch path as an exception from `fn`; this is a sharp edge rather than the ordinary intended call outcome.
`errorFilter` and the failure notification in the catch block are not protected by another local catch. If either throws, that new exception propagates and can supersede the originally caught reason.

accounts.prose: The resolved-value path first applies `resultFilter`. A false result emits success, when observable, and returns `{ success: value }`. A true result is deliberately represented as a handled failure: it emits `onFailure` with `handled: true` and `reason: { value }`, then returns `{ value }`. The thrown/rejected path applies `errorFilter`. A true result emits `handled: true` with `reason: { error }` and returns `{ error }`; a false result emits `handled: false` with the same reason and then rethrows. Synchronous throws and promise rejections converge because the call is awaited inside the `try`.

referent.description: Four classification branches within ExecuteWrapper.invoke

qualifications: The filters are predicates only: they choose the branch but do not replace the resolved or thrown payload.

accounts.prose: Timing is demand-driven. At the start of `invoke`, a stopwatch is created only if either success or failure emitter currently has at least one listener. It uses `performance.now()` when available, otherwise `process.hrtime.bigint()`, and reports milliseconds. The measured interval includes the awaited call and the applicable filter evaluation, ending when the event object is prepared; listener execution itself occurs afterward. No event history is retained by these base emitters.

referent.description: ExecuteWrapper timing and event-observation mechanics

qualifications: If neither emitter has a listener when invocation begins, adding one while the operation is pending does not enable an event for that invocation because the stored stopwatch remains null.

If either emitter has a listener at invocation start, timing is enabled for the invocation even when the eventual outcome belongs to the other emitter; emitting to an emitter with no listeners is a no-op.
Listeners are called synchronously and listener exceptions are not isolated by EventEmitter.

accounts.prose: `clone()` creates a fresh wrapper that reuses the same two predicate function objects but has new success and failure emitters, so listeners are not copied. Separately, `returnOrThrow` converts a completed tagged outcome back to ordinary control flow: `{ error }` is thrown, while both `{ success }` and `{ value }` yield their payload. This separation lets policy implementations inspect handled failures before deciding whether and when to expose a value or throw.

referent.description: ExecuteWrapper cloning and conversion of classified outcomes

qualifications: Sharing predicate functions does not imply copying any external mutable state those functions may close over.

accounts.prose: `ExecuteWrapper.invoke` is a classifier around one function call, not the policy action itself. It starts optional timing, invokes and awaits `fn(...args)`, and then returns exactly one of three tagged shapes: `{ success: value }` for a resolved value rejected by `resultFilter`; `{ value }` for a resolved value accepted by `resultFilter`; or `{ error }` for a caught throw/rejection accepted by `errorFilter`. A caught item rejected by `errorFilter` is not converted into a result: a failure notification is attempted with `handled: false`, then the same thrown value is rethrown. Thus “handled” means selected by a configured filter for policy processing, not that the operation succeeded or that the reason was transformed.

referent.description: Clarified invocation, classification, timing, and notification behavior of ExecuteWrapper

qualifications: This expands the earlier account rather than correcting it; its main outcome classification is consistent with the captured implementation.
The account is based on captured TypeScript source and compiler-derived symbol identity, not execution of the code.

The `try` block also contains result filtering and success/result-failure notification. Consequently, exceptions from `resultFilter` or from listeners invoked there enter the same catch path as an exception from `fn`; this is a sharp edge rather than the ordinary intended call outcome.
`errorFilter` and the failure notification in the catch block are not protected by another local catch. If either throws, that new exception propagates and can supersede the originally caught reason.

accounts.prose: The resolved-value path first applies `resultFilter`. A false result emits success, when observable, and returns `{ success: value }`. A true result is deliberately represented as a handled failure: it emits `onFailure` with `handled: true` and `reason: { value }`, then returns `{ value }`. The thrown/rejected path applies `errorFilter`. A true result emits `handled: true` with `reason: { error }` and returns `{ error }`; a false result emits `handled: false` with the same reason and then rethrows. Synchronous throws and promise rejections converge because the call is awaited inside the `try`.

referent.description: Four classification branches within ExecuteWrapper.invoke

qualifications: The filters are predicates only: they choose the branch but do not replace the resolved or thrown payload.
An unhandled exception can still produce an `onFailure` observation before propagation; “unhandled” means it is not returned as `{ error }`.
With constructor defaults, neither predicate selects anything, so resolved values become `{ success }` and ordinary caught exceptions are rethrown.

accounts.prose: Timing is demand-driven. At the start of `invoke`, a stopwatch is created only if either success or failure emitter currently has at least one listener. It uses `performance.now()` when available, otherwise `process.hrtime.bigint()`, and reports milliseconds. The measured interval includes the awaited call and the applicable filter evaluation, ending when the event object is prepared; listener execution itself occurs afterward. No event history is retained by these base emitters.

referent.description: ExecuteWrapper timing and event-observation mechanics

qualifications: If neither emitter has a listener when invocation begins, adding one while the operation is pending does not enable an event for that invocation because the stored stopwatch remains null.

If either emitter has a listener at invocation start, timing is enabled for the invocation even when the eventual outcome belongs to the other emitter; emitting to an emitter with no listeners is a no-op.
Listeners are called synchronously and listener exceptions are not isolated by EventEmitter.

Separately, `returnOrThrow` converts a completed tagged outcome back to ordinary control flow: `{ error }` is thrown, while both `{ success }` and `{ value }` yield their payload. This separation lets policy implementations inspect handled failures before deciding whether and when to expose a value or throw.

accounts.prose: `ExecuteWrapper.invoke` is a classifier around one function call, not the policy action itself. It starts optional timing, invokes and awaits `fn(...args)`, and then returns exactly one of three tagged shapes: `{ success: value }` for a resolved value rejected by `resultFilter`; `{ value }` for a resolved value accepted by `resultFilter`; or `{ error }` for a caught throw/rejection accepted by `errorFilter`. A caught item rejected by `errorFilter` is not converted into a result: a failure notification is attempted with `handled: false`, then the same thrown value is rethrown. Thus “handled” means selected by a configured filter for policy processing, not that the operation succeeded or that the reason was transformed.

referent.description: Clarified invocation, classification, timing, and notification behavior of ExecuteWrapper

qualifications: This expands the earlier account rather than correcting it; its main outcome classification is consistent with the captured implementation.
The account is based on captured TypeScript source and compiler-derived symbol identity, not execution of the code.

The `try` block also contains result filtering and success/result-failure notification. Consequently, exceptions from `resultFilter` or from listeners invoked there enter the same catch path as an exception from `fn`; this is a sharp edge rather than the ordinary intended call outcome.
`errorFilter` and the failure notification in the catch block are not protected by another local catch. If either throws, that new exception propagates and can supersede the originally caught reason.

accounts.prose: The resolved-value path first applies `resultFilter`. A false result emits success, when observable, and returns `{ success: value }`. A true result is deliberately represented as a handled failure: it emits `onFailure` with `handled: true` and `reason: { value }`, then returns `{ value }`. The thrown/rejected path applies `errorFilter`. A true result emits `handled: true` with `reason: { error }` and returns `{ error }`; a false result emits `handled: false` with the same reason and then rethrows. Synchronous throws and promise rejections converge because the call is awaited inside the `try`.

referent.description: Four classification branches within ExecuteWrapper.invoke

qualifications: The filters are predicates only: they choose the branch but do not replace the resolved or thrown payload.

accounts.prose: Timing is demand-driven. At the start of `invoke`, a stopwatch is created only if either success or failure emitter currently has at least one listener. It uses `performance.now()` when available, otherwise `process.hrtime.bigint()`, and reports milliseconds. The measured interval includes the awaited call and the applicable filter evaluation, ending when the event object is prepared; listener execution itself occurs afterward. No event history is retained by these base emitters.

referent.description: ExecuteWrapper timing and event-observation mechanics

qualifications: If neither emitter has a listener when invocation begins, adding one while the operation is pending does not enable an event for that invocation because the stored stopwatch remains null.

If either emitter has a listener at invocation start, timing is enabled for the invocation even when the eventual outcome belongs to the other emitter; emitting to an emitter with no listeners is a no-op.
Listeners are called synchronously and listener exceptions are not isolated by EventEmitter.

accounts.prose: `clone()` creates a fresh wrapper that reuses the same two predicate function objects but has new success and failure emitters, so listeners are not copied. Separately, `returnOrThrow` converts a completed tagged outcome back to ordinary control flow: `{ error }` is thrown, while both `{ success }` and `{ value }` yield their payload. This separation lets policy implementations inspect handled failures before deciding whether and when to expose a value or throw.

referent.description: ExecuteWrapper cloning and conversion of classified outcomes

qualifications: Sharing predicate functions does not imply copying any external mutable state those functions may close over.

@investigram-7a0a9dfa · interpretation
`ExecuteWrapper.invoke` is a classifier around one function call, not the policy action itself. It starts optional timing, invokes and awaits `fn(...args)`, and then returns exactly one of three tagged shapes: `{ success: value }` for a resolved value rejected by `resultFilter`; `{ value }` for a resolved value accepted by `resultFilter`; or `{ error }` for a caught throw/rejection accepted by `errorFilter`. A caught item rejected by `errorFilter` is not converted into a result: a failure notification is attempted with `handled: false`, then the same thrown value is rethrown. Thus “handled” means selected by a configured filter for policy processing, not that the operation succeeded or that the reason was transformed.
Referent: Clarified invocation, classification, timing, and notification behavior of ExecuteWrapper
  Qualification: This expands the earlier account rather than correcting it; its main outcome classification is consistent with the captured implementation.
  Qualification: The account is based on captured TypeScript source and compiler-derived symbol identity, not execution of the code.
  Qualification: The `try` block also contains result filtering and success/result-failure notification. Consequently, exceptions from `resultFilter` or from listeners invoked there enter the same catch path as an exception from `fn`; this is a sharp edge rather than the ordinary intended call outcome.
  Qualification: `errorFilter` and the failure notification in the catch block are not protected by another local catch. If either throws, that new exception propagates and can supersede the originally caught reason.

@investigram-a94d7314 · interpretation
The resolved-value path first applies `resultFilter`. A false result emits success, when observable, and returns `{ success: value }`. A true result is deliberately represented as a handled failure: it emits `onFailure` with `handled: true` and `reason: { value }`, then returns `{ value }`. The thrown/rejected path applies `errorFilter`. A true result emits `handled: true` with `reason: { error }` and returns `{ error }`; a false result emits `handled: false` with the same reason and then rethrows. Synchronous throws and promise rejections converge because the call is awaited inside the `try`.
Referent: Four classification branches within ExecuteWrapper.invoke
  Qualification: The filters are predicates only: they choose the branch but do not replace the resolved or thrown payload.
  Qualification: An unhandled exception can still produce an `onFailure` observation before propagation; “unhandled” means it is not returned as `{ error }`.
  Qualification: With constructor defaults, neither predicate selects anything, so resolved values become `{ success }` and ordinary caught exceptions are rethrown.

@investigram-e391831d · interpretation
Timing is demand-driven. At the start of `invoke`, a stopwatch is created only if either success or failure emitter currently has at least one listener. It uses `performance.now()` when available, otherwise `process.hrtime.bigint()`, and reports milliseconds. The measured interval includes the awaited call and the applicable filter evaluation, ending when the event object is prepared; listener execution itself occurs afterward. No event history is retained by these base emitters.
Referent: ExecuteWrapper timing and event-observation mechanics
  Qualification: If neither emitter has a listener when invocation begins, adding one while the operation is pending does not enable an event for that invocation because the stored stopwatch remains null.
  Qualification: If either emitter has a listener at invocation start, timing is enabled for the invocation even when the eventual outcome belongs to the other emitter; emitting to an emitter with no listeners is a no-op.
  Qualification: Listeners are called synchronously and listener exceptions are not isolated by EventEmitter.

@investigram-b1cc219c · interpretation
`clone()` creates a fresh wrapper that reuses the same two predicate function objects but has new success and failure emitters, so listeners are not copied. Separately, `returnOrThrow` converts a completed tagged outcome back to ordinary control flow: `{ error }` is thrown, while both `{ success }` and `{ value }` yield their payload. This separation lets policy implementations inspect handled failures before deciding whether and when to expose a value or throw.
Referent: ExecuteWrapper cloning and conversion of classified outcomes
  Qualification: Sharing predicate functions does not imply copying any external mutable state those functions may close over.
  Qualification: The final sentence describes the mechanism enabled by the separation; individual policy decisions were not exhaustively inspected here.

accounts.prose: `ExecuteWrapper.invoke` is a classifier around one function call, not the policy action itself. It starts optional timing, invokes and awaits `fn(...args)`, and then returns exactly one of three tagged shapes: `{ success: value }` for a resolved value rejected by `resultFilter`; `{ value }` for a resolved value accepted by `resultFilter`; or `{ error }` for a caught throw/rejection accepted by `errorFilter`. A caught item rejected by `errorFilter` is not converted into a result: a failure notification is attempted with `handled: false`, then the same thrown value is rethrown. Thus “handled” means selected by a configured filter for policy processing, not that the operation succeeded or that the reason was transformed.

referent.description: Clarified invocation, classification, timing, and notification behavior of ExecuteWrapper

qualifications: This expands the earlier account rather than correcting it; its main outcome classification is consistent with the captured implementation.
The account is based on captured TypeScript source and compiler-derived symbol identity, not execution of the code.

The `try` block also contains result filtering and success/result-failure notification. Consequently, exceptions from `resultFilter` or from listeners invoked there enter the same catch path as an exception from `fn`; this is a sharp edge rather than the ordinary intended call outcome.
`errorFilter` and the failure notification in the catch block are not protected by another local catch. If either throws, that new exception propagates and can supersede the originally caught reason.

accounts.prose: The resolved-value path first applies `resultFilter`. A false result emits success, when observable, and returns `{ success: value }`. A true result is deliberately represented as a handled failure: it emits `onFailure` with `handled: true` and `reason: { value }`, then returns `{ value }`. The thrown/rejected path applies `errorFilter`. A true result emits `handled: true` with `reason: { error }` and returns `{ error }`; a false result emits `handled: false` with the same reason and then rethrows. Synchronous throws and promise rejections converge because the call is awaited inside the `try`.

referent.description: Four classification branches within ExecuteWrapper.invoke

qualifications: The filters are predicates only: they choose the branch but do not replace the resolved or thrown payload.
An unhandled exception can still produce an `onFailure` observation before propagation; “unhandled” means it is not returned as `{ error }`.
With constructor defaults, neither predicate selects anything, so resolved values become `{ success }` and ordinary caught exceptions are rethrown.

accounts.prose: Timing is demand-driven. At the start of `invoke`, a stopwatch is created only if either success or failure emitter currently has at least one listener. It uses `performance.now()` when available, otherwise `process.hrtime.bigint()`, and reports milliseconds. The measured interval includes the awaited call and the applicable filter evaluation, ending when the event object is prepared; listener execution itself occurs afterward. No event history is retained by these base emitters.

referent.description: ExecuteWrapper timing and event-observation mechanics

qualifications: If neither emitter has a listener when invocation begins, adding one while the operation is pending does not enable an event for that invocation because the stored stopwatch remains null.

If either emitter has a listener at invocation start, timing is enabled for the invocation even when the eventual outcome belongs to the other emitter; emitting to an emitter with no listeners is a no-op.
Listeners are called synchronously and listener exceptions are not isolated by EventEmitter.

Separately, `returnOrThrow` converts a completed tagged outcome back to ordinary control flow: `{ error }` is thrown, while both `{ success }` and `{ value }` yield their payload. This separation lets policy implementations inspect handled failures before deciding whether and when to expose a value or throw.

accounts.prose: `ExecuteWrapper.invoke` is a classifier around one function call, not the policy action itself. It starts optional timing, invokes and awaits `fn(...args)`, and then returns exactly one of three tagged shapes: `{ success: value }` for a resolved value rejected by `resultFilter`; `{ value }` for a resolved value accepted by `resultFilter`; or `{ error }` for a caught throw/rejection accepted by `errorFilter`. A caught item rejected by `errorFilter` is not converted into a result: a failure notification is attempted with `handled: false`, then the same thrown value is rethrown. Thus “handled” means selected by a configured filter for policy processing, not that the operation succeeded or that the reason was transformed.

referent.description: Clarified invocation, classification, timing, and notification behavior of ExecuteWrapper

qualifications: This expands the earlier account rather than correcting it; its main outcome classification is consistent with the captured implementation.
The account is based on captured TypeScript source and compiler-derived symbol identity, not execution of the code.

The `try` block also contains result filtering and success/result-failure notification. Consequently, exceptions from `resultFilter` or from listeners invoked there enter the same catch path as an exception from `fn`; this is a sharp edge rather than the ordinary intended call outcome.
`errorFilter` and the failure notification in the catch block are not protected by another local catch. If either throws, that new exception propagates and can supersede the originally caught reason.

accounts.prose: The resolved-value path first applies `resultFilter`. A false result emits success, when observable, and returns `{ success: value }`. A true result is deliberately represented as a handled failure: it emits `onFailure` with `handled: true` and `reason: { value }`, then returns `{ value }`. The thrown/rejected path applies `errorFilter`. A true result emits `handled: true` with `reason: { error }` and returns `{ error }`; a false result emits `handled: false` with the same reason and then rethrows. Synchronous throws and promise rejections converge because the call is awaited inside the `try`.

referent.description: Four classification branches within ExecuteWrapper.invoke

qualifications: The filters are predicates only: they choose the branch but do not replace the resolved or thrown payload.
An unhandled exception can still produce an `onFailure` observation before propagation; “unhandled” means it is not returned as `{ error }`.
With constructor defaults, neither predicate selects anything, so resolved values become `{ success }` and ordinary caught exceptions are rethrown.
