accounts.prose: Timing is demand-driven. At the start of `invoke`, a stopwatch is created only if either success or failure emitter currently has at least one listener. It uses `performance.now()` when available, otherwise `process.hrtime.bigint()`, and reports milliseconds. The measured interval includes the awaited call and the applicable filter evaluation, ending when the event object is prepared; listener execution itself occurs afterward. No event history is retained by these base emitters.

referent.description: ExecuteWrapper timing and event-observation mechanics

qualifications: If neither emitter has a listener when invocation begins, adding one while the operation is pending does not enable an event for that invocation because the stored stopwatch remains null.

If either emitter has a listener at invocation start, timing is enabled for the invocation even when the eventual outcome belongs to the other emitter; emitting to an emitter with no listeners is a no-op.
Listeners are called synchronously and listener exceptions are not isolated by EventEmitter.

accounts.prose: `clone()` creates a fresh wrapper that reuses the same two predicate function objects but has new success and failure emitters, so listeners are not copied. Separately, `returnOrThrow` converts a completed tagged outcome back to ordinary control flow: `{ error }` is thrown, while both `{ success }` and `{ value }` yield their payload. This separation lets policy implementations inspect handled failures before deciding whether and when to expose a value or throw.

referent.description: ExecuteWrapper cloning and conversion of classified outcomes

qualifications: Sharing predicate functions does not imply copying any external mutable state those functions may close over.
The final sentence describes the mechanism enabled by the separation; individual policy decisions were not exhaustively inspected here.

accounts.prose: `ExecuteWrapper.invoke` is a classifier around one function call, not the policy action itself. It starts optional timing, invokes and awaits `fn(...args)`, and then returns exactly one of three tagged shapes: `{ success: value }` for a resolved value rejected by `resultFilter`; `{ value }` for a resolved value accepted by `resultFilter`; or `{ error }` for a caught throw/rejection accepted by `errorFilter`. A caught item rejected by `errorFilter` is not converted into a result: a failure notification is attempted with `handled: false`, then the same thrown value is rethrown. Thus “handled” means selected by a configured filter for policy processing, not that the operation succeeded or that the reason was transformed.

referent.description: Clarified invocation, classification, timing, and notification behavior of ExecuteWrapper

qualifications: This expands the earlier account rather than correcting it; its main outcome classification is consistent with the captured implementation.
The account is based on captured TypeScript source and compiler-derived symbol identity, not execution of the code.

The `try` block also contains result filtering and success/result-failure notification. Consequently, exceptions from `resultFilter` or from listeners invoked there enter the same catch path as an exception from `fn`; this is a sharp edge rather than the ordinary intended call outcome.
`errorFilter` and the failure notification in the catch block are not protected by another local catch. If either throws, that new exception propagates and can supersede the originally caught reason.

accounts.prose: The resolved-value path first applies `resultFilter`. A false result emits success, when observable, and returns `{ success: value }`. A true result is deliberately represented as a handled failure: it emits `onFailure` with `handled: true` and `reason: { value }`, then returns `{ value }`. The thrown/rejected path applies `errorFilter`. A true result emits `handled: true` with `reason: { error }` and returns `{ error }`; a false result emits `handled: false` with the same reason and then rethrows. Synchronous throws and promise rejections converge because the call is awaited inside the `try`.

qualifications: The filters are predicates only: they choose the branch but do not replace the resolved or thrown payload.
An unhandled exception can still produce an `onFailure` observation before propagation; “unhandled” means it is not returned as `{ error }`.
With constructor defaults, neither predicate selects anything, so resolved values become `{ success }` and ordinary caught exceptions are rethrown.

accounts.prose: Timing is demand-driven. At the start of `invoke`, a stopwatch is created only if either success or failure emitter currently has at least one listener. It uses `performance.now()` when available, otherwise `process.hrtime.bigint()`, and reports milliseconds. The measured interval includes the awaited call and the applicable filter evaluation, ending when the event object is prepared; listener execution itself occurs afterward. No event history is retained by these base emitters.

@investigram-7a0a9dfa · interpretation
`ExecuteWrapper.invoke` is a classifier around one function call, not the policy action itself. It starts optional timing, invokes and awaits `fn(...args)`, and then returns exactly one of three tagged shapes: `{ success: value }` for a resolved value rejected by `resultFilter`; `{ value }` for a resolved value accepted by `resultFilter`; or `{ error }` for a caught throw/rejection accepted by `errorFilter`. A caught item rejected by `errorFilter` is not converted into a result: a failure notification is attempted with `handled: false`, then the same thrown value is rethrown. Thus “handled” means selected by a configured filter for policy processing, not that the operation succeeded or that the reason was transformed.
Referent: Clarified invocation, classification, timing, and notification behavior of ExecuteWrapper
  Qualification: This expands the earlier account rather than correcting it; its main outcome classification is consistent with the captured implementation.
  Qualification: The account is based on captured TypeScript source and compiler-derived symbol identity, not execution of the code.
  Qualification: The `try` block also contains result filtering and success/result-failure notification. Consequently, exceptions from `resultFilter` or from listeners invoked there enter the same catch path as an exception from `fn`; this is a sharp edge rather than the ordinary intended call outcome.
  Qualification: `errorFilter` and the failure notification in the catch block are not protected by another local catch. If either throws, that new exception propagates and can supersede the originally caught reason.

@investigram-a94d7314 · interpretation
The resolved-value path first applies `resultFilter`. A false result emits success, when observable, and returns `{ success: value }`. A true result is deliberately represented as a handled failure: it emits `onFailure` with `handled: true` and `reason: { value }`, then returns `{ value }`. The thrown/rejected path applies `errorFilter`. A true result emits `handled: true` with `reason: { error }` and returns `{ error }`; a false result emits `handled: false` with the same reason and then rethrows. Synchronous throws and promise rejections converge because the call is awaited inside the `try`.
Referent: Four classification branches within ExecuteWrapper.invoke
  Qualification: The filters are predicates only: they choose the branch but do not replace the resolved or thrown payload.
  Qualification: An unhandled exception can still produce an `onFailure` observation before propagation; “unhandled” means it is not returned as `{ error }`.
  Qualification: With constructor defaults, neither predicate selects anything, so resolved values become `{ success }` and ordinary caught exceptions are rethrown.

@investigram-e391831d · interpretation
Timing is demand-driven. At the start of `invoke`, a stopwatch is created only if either success or failure emitter currently has at least one listener. It uses `performance.now()` when available, otherwise `process.hrtime.bigint()`, and reports milliseconds. The measured interval includes the awaited call and the applicable filter evaluation, ending when the event object is prepared; listener execution itself occurs afterward. No event history is retained by these base emitters.
Referent: ExecuteWrapper timing and event-observation mechanics
  Qualification: If neither emitter has a listener when invocation begins, adding one while the operation is pending does not enable an event for that invocation because the stored stopwatch remains null.
  Qualification: If either emitter has a listener at invocation start, timing is enabled for the invocation even when the eventual outcome belongs to the other emitter; emitting to an emitter with no listeners is a no-op.
  Qualification: Listeners are called synchronously and listener exceptions are not isolated by EventEmitter.

`clone()` creates a fresh wrapper that reuses the same two predicate function objects but has new success and failure emitters, so listeners are not copied. Separately, `returnOrThrow` converts a completed tagged outcome back to ordinary control flow: `{ error }` is thrown, while both `{ success }` and `{ value }` yield their payload. This separation lets policy implementations inspect handled failures before deciding whether and when to expose a value or throw.

  Qualification: Sharing predicate functions does not imply copying any external mutable state those functions may close over.
  Qualification: The final sentence describes the mechanism enabled by the separation; individual policy decisions were not exhaustively inspected here.

accounts.prose: `ExecuteWrapper.invoke` is a classifier around one function call, not the policy action itself. It starts optional timing, invokes and awaits `fn(...args)`, and then returns exactly one of three tagged shapes: `{ success: value }` for a resolved value rejected by `resultFilter`; `{ value }` for a resolved value accepted by `resultFilter`; or `{ error }` for a caught throw/rejection accepted by `errorFilter`. A caught item rejected by `errorFilter` is not converted into a result: a failure notification is attempted with `handled: false`, then the same thrown value is rethrown. Thus “handled” means selected by a configured filter for policy processing, not that the operation succeeded or that the reason was transformed.

referent.description: Clarified invocation, classification, timing, and notification behavior of ExecuteWrapper

qualifications: This expands the earlier account rather than correcting it; its main outcome classification is consistent with the captured implementation.
The account is based on captured TypeScript source and compiler-derived symbol identity, not execution of the code.

The `try` block also contains result filtering and success/result-failure notification. Consequently, exceptions from `resultFilter` or from listeners invoked there enter the same catch path as an exception from `fn`; this is a sharp edge rather than the ordinary intended call outcome.
`errorFilter` and the failure notification in the catch block are not protected by another local catch. If either throws, that new exception propagates and can supersede the originally caught reason.

accounts.prose: The resolved-value path first applies `resultFilter`. A false result emits success, when observable, and returns `{ success: value }`. A true result is deliberately represented as a handled failure: it emits `onFailure` with `handled: true` and `reason: { value }`, then returns `{ value }`. The thrown/rejected path applies `errorFilter`. A true result emits `handled: true` with `reason: { error }` and returns `{ error }`; a false result emits `handled: false` with the same reason and then rethrows. Synchronous throws and promise rejections converge because the call is awaited inside the `try`.

referent.description: Four classification branches within ExecuteWrapper.invoke

qualifications: The filters are predicates only: they choose the branch but do not replace the resolved or thrown payload.
An unhandled exception can still produce an `onFailure` observation before propagation; “unhandled” means it is not returned as `{ error }`.
With constructor defaults, neither predicate selects anything, so resolved values become `{ success }` and ordinary caught exceptions are rethrown.

accounts.prose: Timing is demand-driven. At the start of `invoke`, a stopwatch is created only if either success or failure emitter currently has at least one listener. It uses `performance.now()` when available, otherwise `process.hrtime.bigint()`, and reports milliseconds. The measured interval includes the awaited call and the applicable filter evaluation, ending when the event object is prepared; listener execution itself occurs afterward. No event history is retained by these base emitters.

referent.description: ExecuteWrapper timing and event-observation mechanics

qualifications: If neither emitter has a listener when invocation begins, adding one while the operation is pending does not enable an event for that invocation because the stored stopwatch remains null.

If either emitter has a listener at invocation start, timing is enabled for the invocation even when the eventual outcome belongs to the other emitter; emitting to an emitter with no listeners is a no-op.
Listeners are called synchronously and listener exceptions are not isolated by EventEmitter.

accounts.prose: `clone()` creates a fresh wrapper that reuses the same two predicate function objects but has new success and failure emitters, so listeners are not copied. Separately, `returnOrThrow` converts a completed tagged outcome back to ordinary control flow: `{ error }` is thrown, while both `{ success }` and `{ value }` yield their payload. This separation lets policy implementations inspect handled failures before deciding whether and when to expose a value or throw.

referent.description: ExecuteWrapper cloning and conversion of classified outcomes

qualifications: Sharing predicate functions does not imply copying any external mutable state those functions may close over.
The final sentence describes the mechanism enabled by the separation; individual policy decisions were not exhaustively inspected here.

accounts.prose: `ExecuteWrapper.invoke` is a classifier around one function call, not the policy action itself. It starts optional timing, invokes and awaits `fn(...args)`, and then returns exactly one of three tagged shapes: `{ success: value }` for a resolved value rejected by `resultFilter`; `{ value }` for a resolved value accepted by `resultFilter`; or `{ error }` for a caught throw/rejection accepted by `errorFilter`. A caught item rejected by `errorFilter` is not converted into a result: a failure notification is attempted with `handled: false`, then the same thrown value is rethrown. Thus “handled” means selected by a configured filter for policy processing, not that the operation succeeded or that the reason was transformed.

referent.description: Clarified invocation, classification, timing, and notification behavior of ExecuteWrapper

qualifications: This expands the earlier account rather than correcting it; its main outcome classification is consistent with the captured implementation.
The account is based on captured TypeScript source and compiler-derived symbol identity, not execution of the code.

The `try` block also contains result filtering and success/result-failure notification. Consequently, exceptions from `resultFilter` or from listeners invoked there enter the same catch path as an exception from `fn`; this is a sharp edge rather than the ordinary intended call outcome.
`errorFilter` and the failure notification in the catch block are not protected by another local catch. If either throws, that new exception propagates and can supersede the originally caught reason.

accounts.prose: The resolved-value path first applies `resultFilter`. A false result emits success, when observable, and returns `{ success: value }`. A true result is deliberately represented as a handled failure: it emits `onFailure` with `handled: true` and `reason: { value }`, then returns `{ value }`. The thrown/rejected path applies `errorFilter`. A true result emits `handled: true` with `reason: { error }` and returns `{ error }`; a false result emits `handled: false` with the same reason and then rethrows. Synchronous throws and promise rejections converge because the call is awaited inside the `try`.

referent.description: Four classification branches within ExecuteWrapper.invoke

qualifications: The filters are predicates only: they choose the branch but do not replace the resolved or thrown payload.
An unhandled exception can still produce an `onFailure` observation before propagation; “unhandled” means it is not returned as `{ error }`.
With constructor defaults, neither predicate selects anything, so resolved values become `{ success }` and ordinary caught exceptions are rethrown.

accounts.prose: Timing is demand-driven. At the start of `invoke`, a stopwatch is created only if either success or failure emitter currently has at least one listener. It uses `performance.now()` when available, otherwise `process.hrtime.bigint()`, and reports milliseconds. The measured interval includes the awaited call and the applicable filter evaluation, ending when the event object is prepared; listener execution itself occurs afterward. No event history is retained by these base emitters.

referent.description: ExecuteWrapper timing and event-observation mechanics

qualifications: If neither emitter has a listener when invocation begins, adding one while the operation is pending does not enable an event for that invocation because the stored stopwatch remains null.

If either emitter has a listener at invocation start, timing is enabled for the invocation even when the eventual outcome belongs to the other emitter; emitting to an emitter with no listeners is a no-op.
Listeners are called synchronously and listener exceptions are not isolated by EventEmitter.

accounts.prose: `clone()` creates a fresh wrapper that reuses the same two predicate function objects but has new success and failure emitters, so listeners are not copied. Separately, `returnOrThrow` converts a completed tagged outcome back to ordinary control flow: `{ error }` is thrown, while both `{ success }` and `{ value }` yield their payload. This separation lets policy implementations inspect handled failures before deciding whether and when to expose a value or throw.

referent.description: ExecuteWrapper cloning and conversion of classified outcomes

qualifications: Sharing predicate functions does not imply copying any external mutable state those functions may close over.
The final sentence describes the mechanism enabled by the separation; individual policy decisions were not exhaustively inspected here.

accounts.prose: `ExecuteWrapper.invoke` is a classifier around one function call, not the policy action itself. It starts optional timing, invokes and awaits `fn(...args)`, and then returns exactly one of three tagged shapes: `{ success: value }` for a resolved value rejected by `resultFilter`; `{ value }` for a resolved value accepted by `resultFilter`; or `{ error }` for a caught throw/rejection accepted by `errorFilter`. A caught item rejected by `errorFilter` is not converted into a result: a failure notification is attempted with `handled: false`, then the same thrown value is rethrown. Thus “handled” means selected by a configured filter for policy processing, not that the operation succeeded or that the reason was transformed.

referent.description: Clarified invocation, classification, timing, and notification behavior of ExecuteWrapper

qualifications: This expands the earlier account rather than correcting it; its main outcome classification is consistent with the captured implementation.
The account is based on captured TypeScript source and compiler-derived symbol identity, not execution of the code.

The `try` block also contains result filtering and success/result-failure notification. Consequently, exceptions from `resultFilter` or from listeners invoked there enter the same catch path as an exception from `fn`; this is a sharp edge rather than the ordinary intended call outcome.
`errorFilter` and the failure notification in the catch block are not protected by another local catch. If either throws, that new exception propagates and can supersede the originally caught reason.

accounts.prose: The resolved-value path first applies `resultFilter`. A false result emits success, when observable, and returns `{ success: value }`. A true result is deliberately represented as a handled failure: it emits `onFailure` with `handled: true` and `reason: { value }`, then returns `{ value }`. The thrown/rejected path applies `errorFilter`. A true result emits `handled: true` with `reason: { error }` and returns `{ error }`; a false result emits `handled: false` with the same reason and then rethrows. Synchronous throws and promise rejections converge because the call is awaited inside the `try`.

referent.description: Four classification branches within ExecuteWrapper.invoke

qualifications: The filters are predicates only: they choose the branch but do not replace the resolved or thrown payload.
An unhandled exception can still produce an `onFailure` observation before propagation; “unhandled” means it is not returned as `{ error }`.
With constructor defaults, neither predicate selects anything, so resolved values become `{ success }` and ordinary caught exceptions are rethrown.

accounts.prose: Timing is demand-driven. At the start of `invoke`, a stopwatch is created only if either success or failure emitter currently has at least one listener. It uses `performance.now()` when available, otherwise `process.hrtime.bigint()`, and reports milliseconds. The measured interval includes the awaited call and the applicable filter evaluation, ending when the event object is prepared; listener execution itself occurs afterward. No event history is retained by these base emitters.

referent.description: ExecuteWrapper timing and event-observation mechanics

qualifications: If neither emitter has a listener when invocation begins, adding one while the operation is pending does not enable an event for that invocation because the stored stopwatch remains null.

If either emitter has a listener at invocation start, timing is enabled for the invocation even when the eventual outcome belongs to the other emitter; emitting to an emitter with no listeners is a no-op.

accounts.prose: `ExecuteWrapper.invoke` is a classifier around one function call, not the policy action itself. It starts optional timing, invokes and awaits `fn(...args)`, and then returns exactly one of three tagged shapes: `{ success: value }` for a resolved value rejected by `resultFilter`; `{ value }` for a resolved value accepted by `resultFilter`; or `{ error }` for a caught throw/rejection accepted by `errorFilter`. A caught item rejected by `errorFilter` is not converted into a result: a failure notification is attempted with `handled: false`, then the same thrown value is rethrown. Thus “handled” means selected by a configured filter for policy processing, not that the operation succeeded or that the reason was transformed.

referent.description: Clarified invocation, classification, timing, and notification behavior of ExecuteWrapper

qualifications: This expands the earlier account rather than correcting it; its main outcome classification is consistent with the captured implementation.
The account is based on captured TypeScript source and compiler-derived symbol identity, not execution of the code.

The `try` block also contains result filtering and success/result-failure notification. Consequently, exceptions from `resultFilter` or from listeners invoked there enter the same catch path as an exception from `fn`; this is a sharp edge rather than the ordinary intended call outcome.
`errorFilter` and the failure notification in the catch block are not protected by another local catch. If either throws, that new exception propagates and can supersede the originally caught reason.

accounts.prose: The resolved-value path first applies `resultFilter`. A false result emits success, when observable, and returns `{ success: value }`. A true result is deliberately represented as a handled failure: it emits `onFailure` with `handled: true` and `reason: { value }`, then returns `{ value }`. The thrown/rejected path applies `errorFilter`. A true result emits `handled: true` with `reason: { error }` and returns `{ error }`; a false result emits `handled: false` with the same reason and then rethrows. Synchronous throws and promise rejections converge because the call is awaited inside the `try`.

referent.description: Four classification branches within ExecuteWrapper.invoke

qualifications: The filters are predicates only: they choose the branch but do not replace the resolved or thrown payload.
An unhandled exception can still produce an `onFailure` observation before propagation; “unhandled” means it is not returned as `{ error }`.
With constructor defaults, neither predicate selects anything, so resolved values become `{ success }` and ordinary caught exceptions are rethrown.

accounts.prose: Timing is demand-driven. At the start of `invoke`, a stopwatch is created only if either success or failure emitter currently has at least one listener. It uses `performance.now()` when available, otherwise `process.hrtime.bigint()`, and reports milliseconds. The measured interval includes the awaited call and the applicable filter evaluation, ending when the event object is prepared; listener execution itself occurs afterward. No event history is retained by these base emitters.

referent.description: ExecuteWrapper timing and event-observation mechanics

qualifications: If neither emitter has a listener when invocation begins, adding one while the operation is pending does not enable an event for that invocation because the stored stopwatch remains null.

If either emitter has a listener at invocation start, timing is enabled for the invocation even when the eventual outcome belongs to the other emitter; emitting to an emitter with no listeners is a no-op.
Listeners are called synchronously and listener exceptions are not isolated by EventEmitter.

accounts.prose: `clone()` creates a fresh wrapper that reuses the same two predicate function objects but has new success and failure emitters, so listeners are not copied. Separately, `returnOrThrow` converts a completed tagged outcome back to ordinary control flow: `{ error }` is thrown, while both `{ success }` and `{ value }` yield their payload. This separation lets policy implementations inspect handled failures before deciding whether and when to expose a value or throw.

referent.description: ExecuteWrapper cloning and conversion of classified outcomes

qualifications: Sharing predicate functions does not imply copying any external mutable state those functions may close over.
The final sentence describes the mechanism enabled by the separation; individual policy decisions were not exhaustively inspected here.

accounts.prose: `ExecuteWrapper.invoke` is a classifier around one function call, not the policy action itself. It starts optional timing, invokes and awaits `fn(...args)`, and then returns exactly one of three tagged shapes: `{ success: value }` for a resolved value rejected by `resultFilter`; `{ value }` for a resolved value accepted by `resultFilter`; or `{ error }` for a caught throw/rejection accepted by `errorFilter`. A caught item rejected by `errorFilter` is not converted into a result: a failure notification is attempted with `handled: false`, then the same thrown value is rethrown. Thus “handled” means selected by a configured filter for policy processing, not that the operation succeeded or that the reason was transformed.

referent.description: Clarified invocation, classification, timing, and notification behavior of ExecuteWrapper

qualifications: This expands the earlier account rather than correcting it; its main outcome classification is consistent with the captured implementation.
The account is based on captured TypeScript source and compiler-derived symbol identity, not execution of the code.

The `try` block also contains result filtering and success/result-failure notification. Consequently, exceptions from `resultFilter` or from listeners invoked there enter the same catch path as an exception from `fn`; this is a sharp edge rather than the ordinary intended call outcome.
`errorFilter` and the failure notification in the catch block are not protected by another local catch. If either throws, that new exception propagates and can supersede the originally caught reason.

accounts.prose: The resolved-value path first applies `resultFilter`. A false result emits success, when observable, and returns `{ success: value }`. A true result is deliberately represented as a handled failure: it emits `onFailure` with `handled: true` and `reason: { value }`, then returns `{ value }`. The thrown/rejected path applies `errorFilter`. A true result emits `handled: true` with `reason: { error }` and returns `{ error }`; a false result emits `handled: false` with the same reason and then rethrows. Synchronous throws and promise rejections converge because the call is awaited inside the `try`.

referent.description: Four classification branches within ExecuteWrapper.invoke

qualifications: The filters are predicates only: they choose the branch but do not replace the resolved or thrown payload.
An unhandled exception can still produce an `onFailure` observation before propagation; “unhandled” means it is not returned as `{ error }`.
With constructor defaults, neither predicate selects anything, so resolved values become `{ success }` and ordinary caught exceptions are rethrown.

accounts.prose: Timing is demand-driven. At the start of `invoke`, a stopwatch is created only if either success or failure emitter currently has at least one listener. It uses `performance.now()` when available, otherwise `process.hrtime.bigint()`, and reports milliseconds. The measured interval includes the awaited call and the applicable filter evaluation, ending when the event object is prepared; listener execution itself occurs afterward. No event history is retained by these base emitters.

referent.description: ExecuteWrapper timing and event-observation mechanics

qualifications: If neither emitter has a listener when invocation begins, adding one while the operation is pending does not enable an event for that invocation because the stored stopwatch remains null.

If either emitter has a listener at invocation start, timing is enabled for the invocation even when the eventual outcome belongs to the other emitter; emitting to an emitter with no listeners is a no-op.
Listeners are called synchronously and listener exceptions are not isolated by EventEmitter.

accounts.prose: `clone()` creates a fresh wrapper that reuses the same two predicate function objects but has new success and failure emitters, so listeners are not copied. Separately, `returnOrThrow` converts a completed tagged outcome back to ordinary control flow: `{ error }` is thrown, while both `{ success }` and `{ value }` yield their payload. This separation lets policy implementations inspect handled failures before deciding whether and when to expose a value or throw.

qualifications: Sharing predicate functions does not imply copying any external mutable state those functions may close over.
The final sentence describes the mechanism enabled by the separation; individual policy decisions were not exhaustively inspected here.

accounts.prose: `ExecuteWrapper.invoke` is a classifier around one function call, not the policy action itself. It starts optional timing, invokes and awaits `fn(...args)`, and then returns exactly one of three tagged shapes: `{ success: value }` for a resolved value rejected by `resultFilter`; `{ value }` for a resolved value accepted by `resultFilter`; or `{ error }` for a caught throw/rejection accepted by `errorFilter`. A caught item rejected by `errorFilter` is not converted into a result: a failure notification is attempted with `handled: false`, then the same thrown value is rethrown. Thus “handled” means selected by a configured filter for policy processing, not that the operation succeeded or that the reason was transformed.

referent.description: Clarified invocation, classification, timing, and notification behavior of ExecuteWrapper

qualifications: This expands the earlier account rather than correcting it; its main outcome classification is consistent with the captured implementation.
The account is based on captured TypeScript source and compiler-derived symbol identity, not execution of the code.

The `try` block also contains result filtering and success/result-failure notification. Consequently, exceptions from `resultFilter` or from listeners invoked there enter the same catch path as an exception from `fn`; this is a sharp edge rather than the ordinary intended call outcome.
`errorFilter` and the failure notification in the catch block are not protected by another local catch. If either throws, that new exception propagates and can supersede the originally caught reason.

accounts.prose: The resolved-value path first applies `resultFilter`. A false result emits success, when observable, and returns `{ success: value }`. A true result is deliberately represented as a handled failure: it emits `onFailure` with `handled: true` and `reason: { value }`, then returns `{ value }`. The thrown/rejected path applies `errorFilter`. A true result emits `handled: true` with `reason: { error }` and returns `{ error }`; a false result emits `handled: false` with the same reason and then rethrows. Synchronous throws and promise rejections converge because the call is awaited inside the `try`.

referent.description: Four classification branches within ExecuteWrapper.invoke

qualifications: The filters are predicates only: they choose the branch but do not replace the resolved or thrown payload.
An unhandled exception can still produce an `onFailure` observation before propagation; “unhandled” means it is not returned as `{ error }`.
With constructor defaults, neither predicate selects anything, so resolved values become `{ success }` and ordinary caught exceptions are rethrown.

accounts.prose: Timing is demand-driven. At the start of `invoke`, a stopwatch is created only if either success or failure emitter currently has at least one listener. It uses `performance.now()` when available, otherwise `process.hrtime.bigint()`, and reports milliseconds. The measured interval includes the awaited call and the applicable filter evaluation, ending when the event object is prepared; listener execution itself occurs afterward. No event history is retained by these base emitters.

referent.description: ExecuteWrapper timing and event-observation mechanics

qualifications: If neither emitter has a listener when invocation begins, adding one while the operation is pending does not enable an event for that invocation because the stored stopwatch remains null.

If either emitter has a listener at invocation start, timing is enabled for the invocation even when the eventual outcome belongs to the other emitter; emitting to an emitter with no listeners is a no-op.
Listeners are called synchronously and listener exceptions are not isolated by EventEmitter.

accounts.prose: ExecuteWrapper.invoke awaits the supplied function. An unfiltered resolved value becomes {success}; a result matching resultFilter becomes handled failure {value}; a thrown value matching errorFilter becomes {error}; and an unhandled throw is rethrown immediately. Success and failure events carry elapsed duration, while failures additionally report handled status and the error/value reason.

qualifications: Both synchronous throws and asynchronous rejection enter the same catch because invocation is awaited inside try/catch.
Default filters reject every error/result, so ordinary results succeed and thrown errors propagate.
